items.name: Readability
items.evidence: Names are clear and there's a docstring, but the dense SIGINT and state-flag logic (sigint_count, was_cancelled, cancelled_workers) has no comments. There's also confusing dead code: `if inspect.isawaitable(coro_or_fut): await coro_or_fut else: await coro_or_fut`.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: run_tasks is one function of about 150 lines (cap: >100 lines is bad). It mixes signal-handler install and restore, worker scheduling and error aggregation. Nested closures share many nonlocal flags, the isawaitable branch is dead, and it reinvents what Semaphore+TaskGroup do.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: It validates max_concurrent and awaits worker cleanup. But signal restore uses `except Exception: pass` and relies on private APIs (`loop._signal_handlers`, `prev_loop_handler._callback`). The custom SIGINT handler raises KeyboardInterrupt from inside a callback, a fragile hack.

items.name: Failures and degenerate arguments
items.evidence: An empty list returns early. `max_concurrent <= 0` raises ValueError. When a task fails, stop_event is set and the other workers are cancelled. The finally block loops on gather until every worker is done, workers stop pulling queued tasks, and first_exception is re-raised.

items.name: Required signature and import behaviour
items.name_zh: 签名与导入行为符合要求
items.evidence: `async def run_tasks(tasks: list[Callable[[], Awaitable[None]]], max_concurrent: int) -> None`. Each callable is invoked lazily by a worker when it pulls the task. Stdlib only, and nothing runs at import; signal handlers are installed only when the function is called.
